Sunﬂower optimization algorithm-based optimal PI control for
enhancing the performance of an autonomous operation of a microgrid
A.M. Hussien, Hany M. Hasanien, S.F. Mekhamer
Electrical Engineering Department, Future University in Egypt, Cairo 11835, Egypt
article info
Article history:
Received 5 September 2020
Revised 10 October 2020
Accepted 12 October 2020
Available online 8 February 2021
Keywords:
Microgrid
Response surface methodology (RSM)
Sunﬂower optimization (SFO)
abstract
This paper presents a novel application of the sunﬂower optimization (SFO) algorithm to enhance the
performance of the inverter based microgrid. The vector cascaded control method is used to control
the inverter which relies on the proportional-integral (PI) controller. The main goal is to select the param-
eters of the PI controller using the SFO algorithm. The multi-objective function for this research is
deduced from the response surface methodology (RSM). The simulation results are tested under three dif-
ferent operating states which are: 1) the system conversion from grid-connected to stand-alone mode, 2)
changing the load during stand-alone mode, and 3) symmetrical fault during stand-alone mode. The
results verify the ﬂexibility, justiﬁcation, and applicability of the presented SFO algorithm versus the par-
ticle swarm optimization (PSO).

1. Introduction
With the growth of the demand, the large centralized generat-
ing stations keep struggling to catch that growth in demands, so
the generation trend now is looking forward to the smaller dis-
tributed generation (DG) systems which are located near to the
load centers. This reduces the transmission losses and decreases
the need to expand the transmission network. The DG systems
importance increased due to their help in enhancing the reliability,
power quality, voltage proﬁle, economic and environmental prof-
its. Mainly, the DG system is capable of:
1) Improving the environment by reduce the carbon emissions
[1–6].
2) Offering convenient solutions to meet the load growth.
3) Decreasing the expansion in the transmission system which
consequently decreases the transmission and distribution
losses.
Additionally, if the DG units are ﬁne controlled, this will
improve the reliability and power quality of the load [7,8].
Due to the growth of DG penetration and the shining of multiple
DG units, the concept of microgrid is brightening up. The microgrid
consists of several DG units and local loads. It can be either grid
connected or standalone (islanded) [9–16]. In the grid connected
mode, the microgrid is connected to the grid. Moreover, the power
balance between the load and generation within the microgrid isn’t
necessary since any power supply shortage will be supplied from
the grid and any overﬂow in the power will be absorbed by the
grid. Meanwhile, in the standalone mode, the microgrid is isolated
from the utility grid. In this mode, the DG controllers have to main-
tain the generation - demand balance and should also maintain the
voltage and frequency within their boundaries.
In the autonomous mode, advanced control strategies are used to
achieve robust and secure operation. Those strategies can be
divided into three main groups: (1) droop-based, (2) centralized
control, and (3) multivariable and servomechanism techniques.
The droop-based one is utilized to manage the ﬂow of the current
of the DG units in an islanded microgrid [17–20]. Droop control
for DC system has enhanced reliability compared to other control
types [21]. The pros of using droop-based control are its capability
to control distributed energy resource (DER) units individually
without creating communication between them. However, its main
disadvantage is inability to handle nonlinear problems such as load
dynamics which affects the system transient response [22–25].O n
the other hand, the centralized control techniques require existence
of high bandwidth communication links and any failure in these

and servomechanism controllers are used in DG units for standalone
mode [28,29]. However, its disadvantage is the high complexity.
Meanwhile, in the nonlinear system, the proportional–integral (PI)
controller is always ﬁrst and pioneer among others because of its
large stability margin. On the other hand, the PI controller faces
great challenge due to the sensitive effect of the parameters tuning.
Therefore, to solve this problem, several meta-heuristic algorithms
have brightened up such as Tabu search [30], biogeography-based
optimization [31,32], gravitational search algorithm (GSA) [33],
harmony search algorithm (HSA) [34], grey wolf optimization and
differential evolution (DE) [35], genetic algorithm (GA) [36–38],
the non-dominated classiﬁcation genetic algorithm-II (NSGA-II)
[39], Taguchi approach [40], Taguchi combined genetic algorithm
(GA) [41], teaching–learning based optimization [42], shufﬂe frog
leaping [43], particle swarm optimization (PSO) [44,45], tree seed
algorithm (TSA) [46], artiﬁcial bee colony (ABC) [47], and salp
swarm algorithm [48]. Each of those techniques has its own advan-
tages and disadvantages [49–51].
In this article, the SFO-based optimal PI controller is introduced
though conventional cascaded control system to improve the per-
formance of an autonomous operation of a microgrid with several
DG units and their loads. The suggested SFO algorithm is chosen to
control the parameters of PI controller. The RSM is utilized to
formulate the ﬁtness function of the optimization. The simulation
results are tested under three different operating states. These
states are: 1) system change from the grid-connected to the
stand-alone, 2) changing the load during the stand-alone, and 3)
symmetrical fault during stand-alone mode. The results verify
the ﬂexibility, justiﬁcation, and applicability of the presented SFO
algorithm versus the particle swarm optimization (PSO). The SFO
algorithm code is constructed by the MATLAB software. The valid-
ity of the introduced system is proved based on simulation results
which are achieved using PSCAD/EMTDC under several operating
scenarios of the microgrid.
2. System model
Fig. 1 represents the single line diagram of a microgrid which
contains 3 DGs connected with each other through transmission
lines. All the DGs are connected to the PCC which is connected to
voltage Source (utility grid) through impedance. Each DG contains
DC voltage Source connected to pulse width modulation (two
level). The PWM is connected to a delta - star connected trans-
former through a series ﬁlter to improve the power quality. The
transformer is connected to a three-phase parallel RLC load which
is used to represent the local load. The microgrid data is presented
in Table 1 .

3. Control strategy
The main reason of DG instability is the disconnection from the
utility grid, which leads to a variation in the ac voltage magnitude
and frequency. The conventional cascaded control scheme for each
DG in the microgrid is presented in the blue dotted box of Fig. 2 .
The direct current (I conv_d) maintains the active power, while the
quadrature current (I conv_q) controls the terminal voltage of each
DG. The reference voltages (V a,V b,Vc) are obtained from the trans-
formation between the dq frame and the stationary frame, the
transformation angle (hPLL) is extracted from the phase-locked loop
(PLL), which uses the grid-side voltages at its input. These refer-
ence voltages are the input of the comparator with 1980 Hz trian-
gular signal to generate the ﬁring pulses of the inverter switches.
Fig. 2 shows the conventional control technique for the grid con-
nected and stand-alone modes [40], [52] and [53] .P conv* is the con-
verter real power reference, P conv is the converter actual real
power, Iconv_d is the inverter direct axis current, I conv_q is the inver-
ter quadrature axis current, V d is the direct axis voltage obtained
from the transformation of the actual terminal voltage, V q is the
quadrature axis voltage obtained from the transformation of the
actual terminal voltage, V conv-d* is the reference direct axis voltage,
and V conv-q* is the reference of quadrature axis voltage.
4. Modeling stage
4.1. The RSM
The importance of the RSM strategy is rapidly increased due to
its success of analyzing different systems. The RSM is considered as
a statistical technique. It constructs models empirically by extract-
ing a correlation between the control parameters and their
response through a statistical decent technique [54–57]. Through
the research study, the PSCAD software helped much in the simu-
lations. It is used to run the RSM model for the scenarios. In this
study, the RSM input data are the maximum percentage overshoots
(MPOS), maximum percentage undershoots (MPUS), steady-state
error (E ss) and settling time (T set) of the terminal voltage proﬁle.
For accurate results, the second-order RSM model is used. The cen-
tral composite design (CCD) technique is used to ﬁt the second-
order RSM model [57]. The MINITAB package [58] is used to run
the RSM model.

4.2. The SFO algorithm
The growth of soft computational capabilities is the key motiva-
tion for using the SFO to ﬁnd solution for the problems to be opti-
mized. The SFO is a population-based heuristic one which is
inspired by the nature. Its main concept is to simulate the sunﬂow-
ers’ orientation to get the radiation of the sun [59]. The sequence of
a sunﬂower is daily periodic. They begin the day with a sun-
tracking movement. At the evening, they go through the reverse
direction. Each sunﬂower is assumed to create only one pollen
gamete. The sunﬂowers directions towards the sun presented in

6. Simulation results and discussion
The simulation of the system is done by PSCAD/EMTDC. Three
scenarios have been tested in this paper. Scenario 1 (STAND ALONE
MODE) starts at t = 2 s. In scenario 2 (variable load mode), R 12 is
changed from 150 O to 300 O at t = 3 s and then back again to
its original value at t = 3.4 s. In the scenario 3, a symmetrical fault
is applied at t = 4 s and is cleared at t = 4.1 s. The scenarios simu-
lation results are introduced in Figs. 4–6 .
PI (1) and PI (2) controllers’ parameters are achieved using PSO
and SFO techniques. The SFO and PSO codes are constructed by the
MATLAB program. The results are represented in Table 10 . They
verify the ﬂexibility, justiﬁcation, and applicability of the pre-
sented SFO algorithm versus the particle swarm optimization
(PSO).

7. Conclusions
This article has presented a new meta-heuristic SFO algorithm
for optimum design scheme of multiple PI controllers’ parameters
to improve the performance of an autonomous operation of a
microgrid with several DG units. Multiple PI controllers are utilized
in conventional cascaded control scheme. The results proved that
the proposed controller is capable of maintaining the active and
reactive power simultaneously as well as tracking the reference
voltages. The results show a rapid and damped transient response
with a small settling time and minimum steady state error under
different operating scheme of the microgrid. The system is tested
under three different operating states which are: 1) system conver-
sion from the grid-connected to the stand-alone mode, 2) changing
